title: What a reported gap is worth

questions.heading: A Constant in the Objective Shrinks the Relative Gap Without Improving the Plan
questions.stem: A model maximizes "total value": $3B for the network that already exists, plus the value of the upgrades it picks, about $30M. Its run reports a relative gap of 0.01%, measured on that total. By roughly how much could the best plan beat the reported one?

options.text: About $3k, since the percentage is taken of the $30M of upgrades
options.says: The solver divides by the incumbent it holds, which includes the $3B; the 0.01% is of about $3.03B.

options.text: Nothing, since a gap of 0.01% marks the plan as the best one
options.says: A gap above zero leaves room for a better plan; 0.01% of the objective is the most it can be worth.

options.text: About $30k, since the gap counts only the upgrades that changed
options.says: The gap is a share of the whole objective, not of the upgrades that differ between plans.

options.text: About $300k, since the percentage is taken of the full $3.03B
options.says: Right: 0.01% of about $3.03B is about $303k, about 1% of the $30M the decisions control.

questions.heading: Plans Within the Gap Can Pick Different Projects
questions.stem: Two runs of a selection model, each stopped at a 0.05% gap, return plans worth 812,400 and 812,300 that share all but six projects. A planner wants to announce that project P31, in the first plan only, "is in the optimal plan". What would support that claim?

options.text: A forced-in run whose incumbent beats a forced-out run's bound
options.says: Right: then some plan with P31 is better than every plan without it, which is what the claim says.

options.text: The first plan being worth more than the second at the same gap
options.says: Both plans are within the gap of the best, so the 100 between them does not show which projects the best plan holds.

options.text: A third run at the same 0.05% gap that again includes P31
options.says: Any number of runs within a tolerance can return near-best plans; none proves which projects the best one holds.

options.text: The gap being smaller than P31's own NPV, so dropping it would show
options.says: Dropping P31 can be offset by adding other projects, as the second-best plan's swap shows.

questions.heading: The Forecast's Error Is Larger Than the Gap
questions.stem: A team solves its nightly plan to a 0.001% gap in 6 hours; at 0.1% it takes 4 minutes. Its NPVs come from forecasts uncertain by several percent. What does that suggest?

options.text: Keep 0.001%, since a smaller gap yields a more valuable plan
options.says: A smaller gap is a closer guarantee on the forecast NPVs; errors in the forecast cost far more than the last fraction of a percent.

options.text: Use the looser gap, since a 0.1% gain sits inside the data's error
options.says: Right: a gap well below the data's error is enough, and the hours are better spent on the forecast or on scenarios.

options.text: Drop the gap for a time limit, since a time limit gives the same plan
options.says: A time limit is not repeatable, and it says nothing about how good the plan is.

options.text: Keep 0.001% only on large runs, since relative gaps grow with size
options.says: A relative gap is a share, so it does not grow with size; the money it stands for does.
